header.askPrompt: What should a veterinary assistant or technician verify before preparing and administering a medication, and when must they stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT?
header.resourcesBody: The SAFE PAWS job aid, your hospital’s medication, hazardous-drug, controlled-substance and sharps policies, product labels and package inserts, the treatment board, and your DVM or RVT.
header.resourcesNote: This lesson teaches verification, preparation, authorized administration, monitoring, documentation, communication and escalation only. overview.heading: You are a safety checkpoint, not an independent prescriber
overview.intro: FDA defines a medication error as a preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of a healthcare professional, patient or consumer — and it places order communication, labeling, compounding, dispensing, administration, education, monitoring and use inside the medication-use process. Most of those steps run through your hands. In a 2024 JAVMA study of a large veterinary teaching hospital, 226 medication errors occurred across 6,155 visits, and 64.2 percent were caught and corrected before reaching the patient. Catching them is the job this lesson teaches.
objectives: Run the Hannah SAFE PAWS check before every medication, in the same order, every time.
Verify a DVM order for completeness: patient, drug, concentration, amount, route, site, frequency, duration and authorization.
Authenticate patient identity against the order and the label before preparation and again at the Pet.
Recognize look-alike and sound-alike names, error-prone abbreviations, trailing zeros and missing leading zeros.
Prepare, label and store medications safely, with hand hygiene, clean technique, sharps safety and integrity checks.
Independently double-check DVM-authorized concentration and dose — and stop and escalate a mismatch instead of recalculating around it.
Apply hazardous-drug and controlled-substance workflows, and audit a controlled-substance log for discrepancies.
Recognize adverse-reaction categories, escalate immediately, document facts and times, and report near-misses.
Deliver a Member teach-back covering what, how much, how often, how long, storage and when to call.
overview.connectsForward: Clinical Diagnostics taught you to protect a sample and support a study. Medication Safety is the first lesson in Clinical Skills & Treatment Delivery because every treatment that follows — fluid therapy, anesthesia support, hospitalized care, emergency shifts — runs on the same verification habit and the same escalation reflex. The SAFE PAWS check and the stop-and-escalate sentence carry into all of them.

modules.title: Why Medication Safety — and the SAFE PAWS Check
modules.completionBody: You have the framework and the boundary. Continue to the foundations module, where you sort what you may verify from what you must escalate.
modules.content:
A medication error is a preventable event that may lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of a healthcare professional, a Member, or a Pet Parent. FDA includes prescribing, order communication, labeling, packaging, nomenclature, compounding, dispensing, distribution, administration, education, monitoring, and use inside that process (FDA CVM). Almost every one of those steps passes through your hands.

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

In this module you will

  • Define medication error and near-miss in Hannah workflow language.
  • Name the eight steps of the Hannah SAFE PAWS medication check and what each one protects against.
  • Locate where error hides at each stage of the medication journey, from order to discharge.
  • State your own boundary: verify, prepare, administer only when authorized, monitor, document, communicate, escalate.

Why it matters

The catch is the job

In a 2024 JAVMA study of a large veterinary teaching hospital, 226 medication errors occurred across 6,155 visits over two years. 64.2 percent were identified and corrected before they reached the patient, and prescribing or order errors were the most frequent category at 58.4 percent (JAVMA, 2024).

In a separate 2025 veterinary teaching-hospital study, medication errors made up 66 percent of incident reports and incorrect dose accounted for 51 percent of those medication errors (2025 study).

Those numbers are the argument for a fixed, boring, repeatable check. The checks in this lesson are what turn an error into a near-miss.

The medication journey

Seven stages, one continuous chain of custody

Every stage below has a documented failure mode. The SAFE PAWS check is designed to be run at the two highest-risk moments: before you prepare, and again at the Pet before anything is given.

1
Order and communication

The DVM decides and communicates. You confirm and clarify.

2
Dispensing and shelf

Right product, right strength, in date, intact, stored correctly.

3
Preparation and labeling

Clean technique, correct measurement, complete label.

4
Administration when authorized

Final identity and order check at the Pet.

5
Monitoring

Watch, recognize, escalate.

6
Documentation

Facts, times, people, response.

7
Member education

Plain language, demonstration, teach-back.

SAFE PAWS step explorer

Interactive practice

Open each letter to see what the step protects against and exactly what you do. Use the arrow keys to move between letters, or Tab to the letter you want and press Enter. The counter tracks how many steps you have opened.

S — Stop and give the order your full attention

Pause what you are doing. Do not read an order while restraining a patient, answering a phone, or holding a conversation.

  • Read the order once end to end before you touch a container.
  • Distraction, fatigue, workload, and preparing syringes ahead of time are documented risk factors for medication error in veterinary practice (2024 review of veterinary anesthesia medication errors).
  • If you are interrupted mid-check, start the check again from the top.
A — Authenticate the Pet, the order, and the authorization

Match the Pet, species, signalment, the weight the order was written on, the encounter, the Member or Pet Parent, and the cage or treatment-board identifier — then confirm the order carries DVM authorization.

  • Say the identifiers out loud and point to each one on the record.
  • Wrong drug, wrong dose, and wrong frequency are reportable medication-error scenarios (FDA adverse-event reporting).
  • No authorization visible means no preparation. Ask, do not assume.
F — Compare formulation, strength, amount, route, and timing to the label

Hold the container next to the order. Compare drug name, active ingredient, concentration or strength, dosage form, amount or volume, route, site if applicable, frequency, and duration.

  • Read the concentration off the label every time, even for a product you use daily.
  • Labeling, packaging, nomenclature, strength display, and dosage-device design are all FDA-identified medication-error contributors (FDA CVM).
  • Look-alike and sound-alike names, generic and brand mismatches, and confusing strength displays all get a read-back (ISMP confused drug names).
E — Escalate anything unclear, missing, mismatched, or outside your role

Hold the medication and go to the DVM or RVT. Escalation is the expected professional behavior, not an interruption.

  • Say what you see, what does not match, and what you need clarified.
  • Do not recalculate around a mismatch, substitute a product, or edit the order.
  • In a 2024 JAVMA study of 226 medication errors, 64.2 percent were caught and corrected before reaching the patient — that catch is this step (JAVMA, 2024).
P — Check allergies, prior reactions, and current status

Confirm documented allergies, prior adverse reactions, current diagnoses, pregnancy or lactation flags, concurrent medications, and species-specific cautions.

  • A new clinical change since the order was written is a reason to pause and ask.
  • Report what is documented; do not interpret an interaction or a contraindication yourself.
  • FDA advises telling the veterinarian about drugs an animal is allergic to or that caused previous problems (FDA).
A — Hand hygiene, clean preparation, PPE, sharps safety

Clean your hands, work in a clean designated preparation area near the time of administration, and apply the hazard controls the product requires.

  • CDC recommends cleaning hands immediately before touching a patient and before an aseptic task (CDC hand hygiene).
  • One needle, one syringe, only one time (CDC injection safety).
  • No PPE or no spill kit for a hazardous drug means you stop and escalate (NIOSH 2010-150).
W — Log, witness, waste, reconcile, secure

For controlled substances, complete the log fields, obtain the required witness, document wasting, reconcile the count, and return the product to secure storage with authorized access only.

  • Never backfill a log or sign for something you did not witness.
  • AAHA controlled-substance logs support DEA recordkeeping and include Schedule II–V logs, opened and unopened container logs, inventory reconciliation, and near-miss incident forms (AAHA).
  • A discrepancy goes to the authorized DVM, RVT, or manager the moment you find it.
S — Document the facts and confirm understanding

Document what was given, by whom, when, route and site, lot and expiration where policy requires it, monitoring and response, Member or Pet Parent education, and any escalation or report.

  • Appropriate dispensing and treatment records must be maintained for veterinary prescription drugs (AVMA).
  • Teach-back is part of the medication, not an extra: ask the Member to tell you the plan back in their own words.
  • Document facts and timing, not conclusions about cause.

Where error hides — click to reveal

Click to reveal

Six stages of the medication journey. Predict the failure mode, then reveal what actually goes wrong there and what your move is.

1. Order and communication

The DVM writes or speaks the order and it reaches you.

Error hides in illegible handwriting, verbal-order mishearing, error-prone abbreviations, trailing zeros, and missing leading zeros. Prescribing and order errors were the largest single category — 58.4 percent — in a 2024 JAVMA study of 226 medication errors across 6,155 visits (JAVMA, 2024).

Your move: read back, ask for full words, and hold anything ambiguous.

2. Shelf and storage

You pull the product from the shelf, fridge, or locked cabinet.

Error hides in look-alike packaging, sound-alike names, multiple strengths of the same drug, expired or damaged stock, broken cold chain, and human medications stored beside animal medications (FDA CVM).

Your move: read the label, not the shape of the box; check expiration and integrity every time.

3. Preparation

You prepare, measure, and label.

Error hides in unlabeled syringes, wrong concentration assumptions, difficult-to-use dosing devices, and syringes prepared far ahead of time. Incorrect dose accounted for 51 percent of medication errors in a 2025 veterinary teaching-hospital study (2025 study).

Your move: label before the syringe leaves your hand, and double-check the ordered math independently.

4. Administration

The medication reaches the Pet.

Error hides in wrong patient, wrong route, wrong site, wrong time, and skipped final pause. FDA places administration inside the medication-use process where errors are counted (FDA CVM).

Your move: repeat the identity and order check cage-side, immediately before you give it — and only when the task is authorized for your role.

5. Monitoring

You watch the Pet after the medication.

Error hides in unwitnessed reactions and in “not acting right” being dismissed. Vomiting, diarrhea, seizures, swelling, and other signs are reportable adverse events (FDA).

Your move: stay with the Pet if it is safe to do so, escalate immediately, and write down what you saw and when.

6. Documentation and discharge

The record is written and the Member takes medication home.

Error hides in missing documentation, vague instructions, and medications stored next to human pills at home. FDA advises never giving human medications to an animal unless the veterinarian directs it, and storing human and animal medications separately (FDA).

Your move: document the facts and use teach-back before the Member leaves.

One boundary, stated once, applied everywhere

Nothing in this lesson authorizes you to diagnose, prescribe, select a medication, choose or change a dose, route, frequency, or duration, substitute a product, or override DVM or RVT direction. Prescription veterinary drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian (AVMA policy).

Your authority is real and it is specific: recognize, verify, prepare, administer when authorized for your role, monitor, document, communicate, and escalate.

  • JAVMA, 2024 — Medication errors in a veterinary teaching hospital (PubMed)
  • Veterinary teaching hospital incident-report study, 2025 (PubMed)
  • Review, 2024 — Medication errors in veterinary anesthesia (PubMed)

  • AVMA — Veterinary Technicians and Veterinary Assistants
  • FDA Consumer Update — Medication Errors Happen to Pets Too

modules.title: Foundations: Scope, Orders and Patient Identity
modules.completionBody: You can now separate verify-and-proceed from clarify-first and hard-stop. Continue to the SAFE PAWS order audit.
modules.content:
You are a safety checkpoint, not an independent prescriber. That sentence is the whole module. Everything you do with a medication either confirms that the DVM’s decision is being carried out exactly, or stops the line so the DVM can decide again.

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

In this module you will

  • State the three response classes for any medication task: proceed as authorized, clarify before preparing, or stop and escalate.
  • List the fields a complete medication order must carry before anything is prepared.
  • Perform a full patient-identity match against the order and the label.
  • Recognize the tasks that require specific authorization for your role.

The order

What “complete” means

AVMA describes the information a veterinary prescription label should carry: veterinarian contact information, the Member or Pet Parent, animal identification, date, drug name and active ingredient, quantity, strength, dosage, route, frequency, duration, refills, cautionary statements, withdrawal times where applicable, and expiration information (AVMA prescriptions FAQ).

For extra-label use, FDA states the labeling must include directions for use covering species and animal identification, dosage, frequency, route, and duration (FDA extra-label resource).

Read that list as your checklist. A field that is missing, illegible, ambiguous, or internally inconsistent is a reason to hold — not a gap for you to fill in.

Proceed as authorized

Every field present and consistent, identity matched, label matched, task authorized for your role. You carry out the order exactly as written.

Clarify before you prepare

Ambiguous abbreviation, trailing zero, missing leading zero, unclear handwriting, verbal order, unclear timing. Hold and clarify with the DVM or RVT, then proceed only on the clarified order.

Stop and escalate now

Concentration or formulation mismatch, missing route or authorization, allergy or reaction flag, expired or damaged product, hazardous drug without PPE, controlled-substance discrepancy, suspected adverse reaction.

Risk sort — proceed, clarify, or stop

Button sort

Twelve medication tasks and findings. Select an item, then choose the lane it belongs in. Nothing is dragged; every control is a button. Check your sort to see the reasoning on every card.

Unsorted items — select one, then choose a lane
Proceed as authorized

Inside your role right now, with the order as written.

    Proceed only with specific authorization

    Requires a role authorization, a witness, or a protocol before you act.

      Stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT

      Hold the medication. Do not correct it yourself.

        Patient identity

        Match the record, not the memory

        Do the identity match twice: once before you prepare, and again at the Pet immediately before anything is given. Say the identifiers out loud and touch each source as you confirm it.

        FDA lists wrong drug, wrong dose, and wrong frequency among the medication-error scenarios that can be reported to the agency (FDA adverse-event reporting). Nearly all of them are preventable at the identity and order match.

        LunaSpecies Canine, spayed femaleAge 4 yrWeight on order 18.0 kgEncounter Treatment — today 10:40Member Ortiz householdAllergy flag: documented reaction to Medication D

        Luna, Milo, Rosie, Jasper, Nori and Scout are teaching cases written for this lesson. Medication names are deliberately generic (“Medication A”), and every number is illustrative teaching data — not a dose recommendation, a reference range, or a Hannah protocol.

        Identity and scope decisions

        Paged decisions

        Four decisions, one at a time, with immediate explanation. This practice is not scored — only the final assessment is.

        • Patient identity

          You are about to prepare an oral medication for Luna. The treatment board says Luna, 18.0 kg. The chart header says Luna, 18.0 kg. The order says Luna, 16.2 kg. What do you do?

        • Patient identity

          Which identity check is strongest before you prepare and again before you administer?

        • Scope

          The DVM order is complete and clearly authorized, but the task — giving an intravenous medication — is not one you are authorized to perform. What is correct?

        • Scope

          A Member asks you at discharge, “What is actually wrong with him?” The DVM has already discussed the plan. What is inside your role?

        Practice complete

        Sources for this module+

modules.title: SAFE PAWS Order Verification Audit
modules.completionBody: You have audited two illustrative orders line by line and practiced read-back. Continue to safe preparation, labeling and storage.
modules.content:
Verification is a line-by-line habit, not a feeling. In this module you audit two illustrative DVM orders field by field, flag every line that does not match, and practice the read-back that defeats look-alike and sound-alike errors.

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

In this module you will

  • Audit an order field by field against the chart, the label, and the product in front of you.
  • Flag a concentration mismatch, a missing route, a missing leading zero, an error-prone abbreviation, and a verbal look-alike risk.
  • Use structured read-back for every verbal order and every ambiguous field.
  • Escalate discrepancies without correcting the order yourself.

Order audit — Luna

Line audit

Eight lines from the order and the product in front of you. Flag every line that does not match or is missing, then check your audit. Two lines need a flag. Each line explains itself after you check.

Case B

Milo — abbreviations, decimals and a verbal addition

Milo is a 4.2 kg neutered male cat. The order below is complete in some fields and dangerous in others. FDA warns that “5.0 mg” can be misread as 50 mg, that “.5 mg” can be misread as 5 mg, and that SID intended as once daily has been misread as BID or QID (FDA).

Order audit — Milo

Line audit

Seven lines. Three need a flag. Watch the numbers and the abbreviations as closely as the drug name.

Read-back and number-safety decisions

Paged decisions

Four decisions on verbal orders, trailing zeros, look-alike products, and frequency conflicts.

  • Read-back

    A DVM gives you a verbal medication order across the treatment room while you are restraining a cat. What is the safe sequence?

  • Numbers

    An order reads “5.0 mg”. What is the safest response?

  • Look-alike, sound-alike

    Two products on the shelf have near-identical packaging and similar names, and both are stocked in two strengths. What controls the risk at the moment you pull one?

  • Timing

    An order reads “q24h” but the treatment board shows two administration slots for today. What do you do?

Practice complete

What escalation sounds like

Say: “I am holding Luna’s Medication A. The order reads 50 mg per mL and the bottle on the tray reads 25 mg per mL, and the route is not written. I have not prepared anything. Can you confirm the intended concentration, volume and route?”

Do not say: “The bottle is half strength so I doubled the volume.” That is prescribing, and it is outside your role.

modules.title: Safe Preparation, Labeling and Storage
modules.completionBody: You sequenced a clean preparation, built a complete label, and worked storage and sharps exceptions. Continue to the independent double-check.
modules.content:
Preparation is where a correct order becomes a correct syringe — or does not. Incorrect dose accounted for 51 percent of medication errors in a 2025 veterinary teaching-hospital study (2025 study), and preparing syringes ahead of time is a named risk factor in veterinary anesthesia error reviews (2024 review).

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

In this module you will

  • Sequence a clean medication preparation from stopped surface to documented disposal.
  • Build a complete prepared-medication label with every required field.
  • Check expiration, beyond-use, integrity, storage, and cold chain, and escalate exceptions.
  • Apply sharps and injection-safety rules, including exposure reporting.

Medication-prep tray — put the steps in order

Sequence

Eight preparation steps, deliberately out of order. Click the step you would do next. A step chosen too early explains why it comes later and stays available. Reset the tray at any time.

Preparation surface — choose the next correct step
Your sequence so far
    Clean preparation, in order

    Stopped surface, clean hands, order-to-label match, identity and allergy check, product inspection, measure exactly as ordered, label before it leaves your hand, dispose and document. Run the same order every time so that a missing step is obvious.

    Labeling

    Every prepared medication is labeled before it leaves your hand

    FDA identifies labeling, packaging, nomenclature, and dosage-device design as medication-error contributors (FDA CVM). An unlabeled syringe on a tray is an anonymous medication, and anonymous medications get given to the wrong patient.

    Build the label below line by line. A wrong option explains itself and stays available; a correct option is added to the live label.

    Label builder — Luna’s clarified order

    Builder

    Five label lines. The DVM has now issued a corrected order for the product you actually have: Medication A oral suspension, 25 mg/mL — 180 mg PO once now, which is 7.2 mL. Choose the safest wording for each line.

    Line 1 — patient

    Which patient line makes the syringe unambiguous at the cage in three months of charts?

    Line 2 — drug and concentration

    How do you write the medication and strength?

    Line 3 — amount and route

    The corrected DVM order authorizes 7.2 mL PO. How is that written?

    Line 4 — time and preparer

    What time-and-person information belongs on the label?

    Line 5 — beyond-use and cautions

    The last line on the label carries what?

    Prepared-medication label

    Nothing added yet. Choose the first option to start.

      Label complete

      Patient, drug and concentration, amount and route, time and preparer, beyond-use and caution. Five lines, no abbreviations that can be misread, no trailing zeros, no missing leading zeros. This label can be read out loud at the cage as your final check.

      Storage, integrity and exposure — click to reveal

      Click to reveal

      Six shelf-and-fridge situations. Decide your move, then reveal the rule and the escalation.

      Expiration and beyond-use

      A vial is in date on the box, opened three weeks ago. Is it usable?

      Check both: the manufacturer expiration and the beyond-use date set by policy once the container is opened or the product is reconstituted. Whichever comes first wins.

      Escalate if the beyond-use date is missing, unclear, or passed. Quarantine the product; do not dispense from it.

      Integrity

      The suspension looks slightly darker than you remember and there is a fine sediment.

      Do not shake it and hope. Product defects are an FDA-recognized medication-error contributor (FDA CVM). Set it aside, label it as quarantined, and escalate.

      Report product problems through your hospital process; FDA also accepts reports of product defects.

      Cold chain

      The refrigerator log shows a two-hour gap and reads 4 degrees above the acceptable range.

      Temperature excursion. Do not use or dispense affected product on your own judgment. Escalate to the DVM, RVT, or manager, keep the product separated, and document the log finding and the times.

      FDA advises storing medications per label conditions and keeping labels intact (FDA safe storage).

      Human and animal separation

      A Member asks if they can keep their dog’s chewables in their own pill organizer.

      No. FDA advises storing human and animal medications separately to prevent mix-ups, keeping pet medications in their original labeled containers, and storing them securely away from Pets and children (FDA).

      Flavored chewables are attractive to Pets, and a container left within reach is an overdose waiting to happen.

      Human medication exposure

      A Member mentions using a topical cream from their own prescription on a lesion.

      Stop and route it to the DVM immediately. FDA warns that topical fluorouracil products intended for people can be deadly to dogs and cats even after small exposures (FDA fluorouracil warning).

      Do not advise on human medications. Document the exposure history and escalate.

      Secure storage and access

      A controlled-substance vial is on the counter while you finish a task.

      Controlled substances live in locked storage with access limited to authorized personnel, and they return there immediately. An unattended controlled substance is a chain-of-custody break and a reportable discrepancy.

      Log, witness, waste, reconcile, secure — the W step of SAFE PAWS (AAHA controlled-substance logs).

      Sharps and injection-safety decisions

      Paged decisions

      Three decisions on disposal, single-use practice, and exposure reporting.

      • Sharps

        You have just given an injection the RVT authorized you to give. The sharps container is across the room. What do you do?

      • Injection safety

        What does “One Needle, One Syringe, Only One Time” require?

      • Exposure

modules.title: The Independent Double-Check: Concentration, Dose, Route
modules.completionBody: You verified authorized math, refused an unauthorized substitution, and held route and formulation boundaries. Continue to hazardous drugs and controlled substances.
modules.content:
You verify the ordered math. You never choose it. Every calculation in this module exists so that you can say one of two sentences: “this matches the authorized order” or “this does not match, I have prepared nothing, and I need direction.”

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

Authorization boundary for every calculation in this lesson

The dose, the concentration, the route, the frequency and the duration are all decided by the DVM. Your calculation is a verification of an existing authorized order and an independent double-check — never dose selection, never a substitution, never a workaround for a product mismatch.

Prescription veterinary drugs are restricted to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian (AVMA policy), and technicians and assistants cannot prescribe or diagnose (AVMA).

In this module you will

  • Restate an authorized order in full before touching a container.
  • Read concentration from the container in your hand, every time.
  • Verify the DVM-authorized math independently and describe the result in the order's own terms.
  • Refuse to recalculate around a concentration or formulation mismatch, and escalate instead.
  • Hold route, site, formulation, and timing exactly as ordered.

How the math is used here

Two sentences, one boundary

The arithmetic is simple on purpose: dose in milligrams divided by concentration in milligrams per millilitre gives the volume. What matters is what you do with the answer.

If your independent check agrees with the authorized order and the task is authorized for your role, you carry it out. If it does not agree — for any reason, including a product that is a different strength — you stop, prepare nothing, and escalate. There is no third option.

1
Restate the authorized order

Drug, concentration, dose, route, timing, and who authorized it — read from the order.

2
Read the container

Concentration and formulation come from the label in your hand, not from habit.

3
Verify the ordered math

Dose ÷ concentration = volume. Leading digit, no trailing zero.

4
Independent second check

A second qualified person re-derives it without seeing your answer.

5
Match, or stop

Match: carry out the order as written, if authorized for your role. Mismatch: prepare nothing and escalate.

LunaSpecies CanineWeight on order 18.0 kgOrder Medication A oral suspensionAll values illustrative teaching data

Concentration and dose double-check — the matching case

Double-check

Five checkpoints on an order that does match. Choose the safe action at each step; wrong options explain themselves and stay available.

Step 1 — restate the authorized order

What exactly did the DVM authorize? Read it from the order, not from memory.

Step 2 — read the concentration off the container

The bottle in your hand says what?

Step 3 — verify the ordered math independently

180 mg at 25 mg/mL. What volume does the authorized order work out to?

Step 4 — have a second person check

You have a volume that matches. What is the next safety step before administration?

Step 5 — decide what happens next

Everything matches and the task is authorized for your role. What is your action?

Your double-check record

Nothing added yet. Choose the first option to start.

    Double-check complete — and it matched

    180 mg ÷ 25 mg/mL = 7.2 mL, verified independently by a second qualified team member, administered exactly as authorized. Note what you never did: you did not choose the dose, change the route, or round for convenience.

    The mismatch case — where the arithmetic must not be used

    Double-check

    Same medication, a different day, and a strength that does not match the order. Four steps. The tempting answer is the wrong one.

    Step 1 — name what does not match

    Same patient, different day. The order reads 180 mg at 50 mg/mL — 3.6 mL; the only bottle in stock reads 25 mg/mL. What do you write down?

    Step 2 — decide whether to recalculate

    You can see that 180 mg at 25 mg/mL would be 7.2 mL. Do you prepare it?

    Step 3 — escalate in words

    How do you hand this to the DVM or RVT?

    Step 4 — close the loop

    The DVM issues a corrected order. What now?

    Your escalation record

    Nothing added yet. Choose the first option to start.

      Correctly escalated

      You could do the arithmetic. You did not use it, because using it would have substituted a different concentration on your own authority. FDA identifies inconsistent strength presentation and label confusion as medication-error contributors; the safe response is a held medication and a clear escalation.

      Route, formulation, site and timing decisions

      Paged decisions

      Four decisions where the pressure is to be helpful. Each one belongs to the prescriber.

      • Route

        An order reads “Medication C 10 mg PO q12h”. The Pet is refusing tablets and a colleague suggests giving the injectable form instead. What is correct?

      • Formulation

        The order specifies an oral suspension. Only tablets of the same drug are in stock. What do you do?

      • Site

        An injection the RVT authorized you to give specifies a site you cannot use because the area is inflamed. What is correct?

      • Timing

        You are 90 minutes late to a q12h dose because of an emergency. What is the safe action?

      Practice complete

      Sources for this module+

      • AVMA — Veterinary Technicians and Veterinary Assistants
      • FDA CVM — Veterinary Medication Errors
      • FDA — The Ins and Outs of Extra-Label Drug Use in Animals
      • Veterinary teaching hospital incident-report study, 2025 (PubMed)
      • FDA — All Creatures Great and Small: Properly Medicate Them All

modules.title: Hazardous Drugs, PPE and Controlled Substances
modules.completionBody: You worked PPE decisions and audited a controlled-substance log. Continue to the capstone: administration, monitoring, escalation and teach-back.
modules.content:
Two medication categories carry rules beyond the standard check: hazardous drugs, which can harm the people handling them, and controlled substances, which carry legal chain-of-custody obligations. In both, “I could not follow the protocol so I improvised” is the failure mode.

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

In this module you will

  • Identify hazardous-drug status and apply the hospital hazardous-drug workflow, PPE, and disposal pathway.
  • Stop and escalate when PPE, engineering controls, or spill supplies are unavailable.
  • Audit a controlled-substance log for missing patient, missing witness, and reconciliation problems.
  • Report a controlled-substance discrepancy through the authorized route without backfilling records.

Hazardous drugs and controlled substances — click to reveal

Click to reveal

Four questions people actually ask. Reveal the standard and what it means for your shift.

What makes a drug “hazardous” here

Is it about the patient or the team?

Both, and the environment. USP General Chapter <800> applies to handling hazardous drugs where patients, healthcare workers, or the environment may be exposed (USP <800> FAQ, January 2026). NIOSH identifies the 2024 NIOSH List as the current list and includes veterinary care workers among potentially exposed healthcare workers (NIOSH).

Your move: know how your hospital flags hazardous products, and treat the flag as a workflow instruction, not a warning label.

Why veterinary practices are covered

“That guidance is for human hospitals.”

OSHA states its hazardous-drug guidance applies to veterinary practices because many drugs used in people are also used to treat animals (OSHA), and NIOSH has published guidance specifically for veterinary healthcare employees (NIOSH 2010-150).

Your move: follow the hospital hazardous-drug program exactly as written, and escalate gaps rather than working around them.

Controlled substances — what the log is for

Why so many fields for one small volume?

AAHA states its controlled-substance logs support DEA recordkeeping requirements and include Schedule II–V logs, unopened and opened container logs, inventory reconciliation, near-miss incidents, expired substances, and initial and biennial inventory forms (AAHA).

Your move: complete every field at the moment of the action, with the required witness. A log completed later is a log you cannot defend.

Prescription monitoring context

Does anything get reported outside the hospital?

Requirements are state-specific. In Oregon, from January 1, 2025, licensed pharmacy outlets must report certain veterinarian-prescribed controlled substances and gabapentin to the state PDMP, while veterinary practices dispensing directly continue their existing state and DEA recording practices (Oregon Veterinary Medical Examining Board).

Your move: follow your own state's rules and Hannah policy. Ask your manager which apply at your location.

PPE and hazardous-drug scenarios

Scenario decisions

Four scenarios: a hazardous oral medication, a hazardous injectable, a spill, and a routine non-hazardous medication for contrast. One at a time, with the rationale after each choice.

  • Hazardous oral medication

    Rosie is an oncology recheck. You are asked to assist with handling a prescribed hazardous oral medication package. The hospital hazardous-drug protocol calls for designated PPE and a designated handling area. The PPE box is empty. What do you do?

  • Hazardous injectable

    A hazardous injectable is to be prepared. Which statement reflects the correct approach for a learner at your level?

  • Spill

    A small volume of a hazardous drug spills on the floor. The spill kit is not where it should be. What is correct?

  • Non-hazardous comparison

    A routine, non-hazardous oral medication is being dispensed. Which controls still apply?

Practice complete

Case D

Jasper — controlled substance, procedure day

A controlled medication was removed from locked storage for Jasper's procedure. Audit the eight log lines below and flag every line that is incomplete or does not reconcile. Two lines need a flag.

JasperSpecies CanineEncounter Procedure dayStorage Locked cabinet, authorized accessControlled substance — chain of custody in effect
Controlled-substance log — opened containerChain of custody
ProductControlled medication, Schedule reference per hospital log
Drawn2.0 mL
Administered1.4 mL
Wasted0.6 mL
Witness— not recorded —
Patient— not recorded —
Discrepancyescalate now

Controlled-substance log audit

Log audit

Eight log lines. Flag the lines that are incomplete or do not reconcile, then check your audit.

Never do these four things with a controlled-substance log

Do not backfill a missing field from memory. Do not sign as a witness for something you did not see. Do not ask a colleague to sign retrospectively. Do not delay reporting a discrepancy to “see if it resolves.”

AAHA’s controlled-substance materials include near-miss incident forms precisely because discrepancies are expected to be reported and learned from (AAHA controlled-substance FAQs).

modules.title: Administer, Monitor, Escalate and Teach Back
modules.completionBody: You escalated an adverse reaction, reported a near-miss, built a Member teach-back, stepped through the full recap, and have the printable job aid. Continue to the final assessment.
modules.content:
This is the capstone. Two branching cases, a Member teach-back, the full SAFE PAWS recap, a competency self-validation checklist, and a one-page job aid you can print and keep at the preparation area.

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

In this module you will

  • Recognize adverse-reaction categories and escalate immediately with facts and times.
  • Preserve evidence and document observations without naming a cause.
  • Respond to a near-miss using just-culture reporting rather than concealment.
  • Deliver a Member teach-back covering what, how much, how often, how long, storage and when to call.
  • Self-assess against the medication-safety competencies and print the SAFE PAWS job aid.

The cage-side pause

The last checkpoint before anything is given

At the Pet, immediately before administration, repeat the identity and order out loud: Pet, medication, concentration, amount, route and site, time, and order status. Then ask yourself one more question: has anything changed since the order was written?

A new clinical change, a new Member concern, a new allergy note, or a patient who simply is not acting right all stop the administration and go back to the DVM or RVT. FDA places administration and monitoring inside the medication-use process where errors are counted (FDA CVM).

What you see

Name the observable change: what, where, when, how much, how long.

Why it matters

It followed a medication, or it conflicts with the plan. That is enough to act.

What you do

Stay with the Pet if safe, escalate immediately, preserve evidence, note times.

Who you notify

DVM or RVT now. Then documentation and the internal report per policy.

NoriSpecies FelineEncounter Post-medication observationGiven 1.8 mL PO at 10:52Suspected adverse reaction — escalate

Case E — Nori: adverse-reaction escalation simulation

Branching case

Four decisions in sequence. A wrong choice explains itself and stays available so you can correct it; a correct choice is added to your action log and advances the case.

Stage 1 — something changes

Nori is a feline patient under post-medication observation. Twelve minutes after an authorized medication, she vomits, you can see facial swelling around the muzzle, and she is suddenly restless and trying to hide. What is your first action?

Stage 2 — while help is coming

You have called out and the RVT is on the way. What do you do in the next thirty seconds?

Stage 3 — the DVM arrives

The DVM asks what happened. What do you say?

Stage 4 — after the immediate response

The DVM has taken over care and directs you to document. What goes in the record and where does the report go?

Actions you have taken
    Case complete

    Recognized, escalated immediately, preserved the physical evidence, reported facts and times, and documented without naming a cause. That is the whole job in an adverse-reaction event.

    Case A revisited — near-miss response and just-culture reporting

    Branching case

    You caught a concentration mismatch before it reached Luna. Four decisions about what happens next, from the catch to what changes afterwards.

    Stage 1 — the catch

    You are preparing Luna’s medication. The order reads 50 mg/mL; the bottle in your hand reads 25 mg/mL. Nothing has been given. You have four minutes before the treatment round moves on. What do you do?

    Stage 2 — who hears about it

    The DVM issues a corrected order and Luna gets the right medication. The near-miss reached no patient. What now?

    Stage 3 — what goes in the report

    You are filling in the near-miss report. Which version is right?

    Stage 4 — what changes

    Your report is reviewed. What is the appropriate learning response to a near-miss like this?

    Actions you have taken
      Near-miss handled well

      Caught before preparation, escalated instead of substituting, reported internally with facts and the system condition, and treated as team learning. FDA encourages reporting medication errors even when no adverse event occurred, so patterns can be found and prevented (FDA CVM — veterinary medication errors).

      Member communication

      Discharge is a safety step, not a formality

      The Member or Pet Parent becomes the person administering this medication. FDA's guidance for them is built around four questions: what does the drug treat, how much and how often and how long do I give it, how do I store it, and what side effects should I watch for (FDA — medication errors happen to pets too).

      You deliver the DVM's written instructions in plain language, show the product and the dosing device, cover storage, name what should prompt a call, and then ask for teach-back. Human medications are a specific risk: FDA advises Members and Pet Parents not to give human medication to an animal unless the veterinarian directs it, and to store human and animal medications separately to prevent mix-ups (FDA — properly store medications). Some human products are dangerous even in small exposures — FDA warns that topical fluorouracil products made for people can be deadly to dogs and cats (FDA — topical fluorouracil warning).

      ScoutSpecies CanineVisit DischargeGoing home with Flavored chewable, DVM-written instructions

      Case F — Scout: build the Member teach-back

      Teach-back builder

      Six lines, one at a time. Each correct choice is added to your discharge script; a wrong choice explains why and lets you try again.

      Line 1 — open with the plan

      Scout is going home with a flavored chewable medication. How do you open?

      Line 2 — show, do not just tell

      What do you do with the medication itself?

      Line 3 — storage

      What storage guidance belongs in this conversation?

      Line 4 — the human-medication question

      The Member asks: “Can I keep these next to my own pills so I remember? And can I give him one of my pain relievers if he seems sore?”

      Line 5 — what to watch for and when to call

      How do you close?

      Line 6 — teach-back

      The last step before the Member leaves is what?

      Your discharge script

      Nothing added yet. Choose the first option to start.

        Teach-back script complete

        Plain language, the product in view, storage, the human-medication boundary, monitoring and the escalation route — and then the Member restating the plan in their own words. Nothing in this script creates or changes an instruction.

        Progressive recap — the whole lesson in ten points

        Step-through recap

        Step through the SAFE PAWS workflow and the two response rules one point at a time. Move back and forth as much as you like.

        • S — Stop

          Pause and give the order your full attention. No multitasking during a medication check, and if you are interrupted, start the check again.

        • A — Authenticate

          Pet, species, signalment, the weight the order was written on, encounter, Member or Pet Parent, cage or board identifier, and visible DVM authorization — matched twice: before preparation and again at the Pet.

        • F — Formulation and concentration

          Compare drug, active ingredient, concentration, dosage form, amount, route, site, frequency and duration to the container label in your hand. Read the label, not the shape of the box.

        • E — Escalate

          Anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, unlabeled or outside your role stops the line. Prepare nothing, and never recalculate around a mismatch.

        • P — Patient and allergy status

          Documented allergies, prior adverse reactions, current status, pregnancy or lactation flags, concurrent medications, and species cautions. Report them; do not interpret them.

        • A — Aseptic and hazard controls

          Hand hygiene before the aseptic task and before patient contact; clean designated preparation area; one needle, one syringe, only one time; hazardous-drug PPE and workflow or you stop.

        • W — Witness and chain of custody

          Controlled substances: complete every log field at the time of the action, obtain the required witness, document wasting, reconcile the count, and return to secure storage. Never backfill.

        • S — Sign, document, teach back

          Document what was given, by whom, when, route and site, lot and expiration per policy, monitoring and response, Member education, and any escalation or report. Then teach back.

        • Recognize and escalate

          Acute distress, collapse, vomiting or diarrhea, swelling or hives, seizures, respiratory changes, injection-site reactions, unexpected sedation or excitation, and “not acting right” all go to the DVM or RVT immediately.

        • Report near-misses

          A catch is a system signal. Report it with facts, times and the condition that made it possible — FDA encourages reporting medication errors even when no adverse event occurred.

        Recap complete

        All ten points revealed. If any of them felt unfamiliar, re-open that module before your next medication task — the final assessment covers all eight domains.

        Competency self-validation

        Competency validation

        Check each statement you are ready to be observed doing. This checklist is ungraded and is not saved — it is a conversation starter with your DVM or RVT preceptor, and self-assessment never replaces observed validation.

        Printable one-page job aid

        Job aid

        The card below is the whole workflow on one page. Print it and keep it at the preparation area. It prints on its own, without the rest of the app.

        SAFE PAWS — before every medication

        Hannah Learning System — Medication Safety job aid · illustrative teaching tool, not a protocol
        S — StopPause. No multitasking. Interrupted means start again.
        A — AuthenticatePet, species, weight on the order, encounter, Member, cage ID, DVM authorization.
        F — Formulation and concentrationDrug, ingredient, strength, form, amount, route, site, frequency, duration — against the label in your hand.
        E — EscalateUnclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role: hold it. Prepare nothing.
        P — Patient and allergy statusAllergies, prior reactions, current status, concurrent medications, species cautions.
        A — Aseptic and hazard controlsHand hygiene, clean prep area, one needle one syringe one time, PPE and hazardous-drug workflow.
        W — Witness and chainControlled substances: log, witness, waste, reconcile, secure. Never backfill.
        S — Sign, document, teach backWhat, who, when, route and site, monitoring, Member education, escalation and reports.
        Stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT when you see: missing Pet ID, route, frequency, concentration, dose or volume, duration or authorization · a different concentration, strength or formulation than ordered · allergy, prior reaction, new clinical change or Member concern · look-alike or sound-alike risk, unclear abbreviation, trailing zero, missing leading zero, illegible or verbal ambiguity · expired, damaged, unlabeled, improperly stored or questionable integrity · hazardous drug without required PPE or workflow · controlled-substance discrepancy, missing witness or field, or unsecured access · needle-stick, spill, exposure, adverse reaction, wrong drug, dose or frequency, or any near-miss.

        You never: diagnose, prescribe, select a medication, choose or change a dose, route, frequency or duration, substitute a product, or recalculate around a mismatch.

        Sources and framework credits

        SAFE PAWS is a Hannah-branded memory aid for safe medication workflow behavior, assembled for this lesson from the public standards below. It is not a clinical rule, a prescribing algorithm, or a published framework.

        • Medication-error definition, causes and reporting — FDA CVM — Veterinary Medication Errors
        • Adverse-event and problem reporting, including medication errors and needle-stick exposure (2026) — FDA — How to Report Animal Drug and Device Side Effects and Product Problems (2026)
        • Member and Pet Parent medication-error guidance, look-alike/sound-alike example — FDA Consumer Update — Medication Errors Happen to Pets Too
        • Abbreviations, trailing zeros and missing leading zeros — FDA — All Creatures Great and Small: Properly Medicate Them All
        • Storage, labeling and human/animal separation — FDA — Properly Store Medications to Keep Your Pet Safe
        • Topical fluorouracil exposure warning — FDA — Don’t Expose Pets to Prescription Topical Fluorouracil
        • Extra-label directions for use — FDA — The Ins and Outs of Extra-Label Drug Use in Animals
        • Prescription-drug authority and VCPR — AVMA policy — Use of Prescription Drugs in Veterinary Medicine
        • Technician and assistant scope — AVMA — Veterinary Technicians and Veterinary Assistants
        • Prescription label fields — AVMA — Prescriptions and Pharmacies FAQs for Veterinarians
        • Hand hygiene — CDC — Hand Hygiene in Healthcare Settings
        • Injection safety — CDC — Injection Safety: One Needle, One Syringe, Only One Time
        • Sharps and needlestick prevention — OSHA — Bloodborne Pathogens and Needlestick Prevention, General Guidance
        • Hazardous drugs in veterinary practice — NIOSH 2010-150 — Hazardous Drugs in Veterinary Healthcare; NIOSH — Hazardous Drugs in Healthcare (2024 NIOSH List); OSHA — Controlling Occupational Exposure to Hazardous Drugs; USP General Chapter <800> FAQ, January 2026
        • Controlled-substance logs and chain of custody — AAHA — Controlled Substance Logs and Resources; AAHA — Controlled Substance FAQs
        • Confused drug names — ISMP — List of Confused Drug Names
        • State prescription-monitoring context — Oregon Veterinary Medical Examining Board — PDMP guidance (effective January 1, 2025)
        • Veterinary medication-error evidence — JAVMA, 2024 — Medication errors in a veterinary teaching hospital (PubMed); Veterinary teaching hospital incident-report study, 2025 (PubMed); Review, 2024 — Medication errors in veterinary anesthesia (PubMed)

        Clinical review required before production use. This lesson was assembled from public regulatory and professional sources and must be reviewed and approved by Hannah clinical leadership before release. All patients, orders, medication names, concentrations, volumes and log entries are illustrative teaching data written for instruction — they are not dose recommendations, reference ranges, product guidance or Hannah protocols. Learners must follow their own hospital policy, DVM and RVT direction, and applicable state practice act and DEA requirements, which take precedence over anything shown here.

        Sources for this module+
        • FDA CVM — Veterinary Medication Errors
        • FDA — How to Report Animal Drug and Device Side Effects and Product Problems (2026)
        • FDA Consumer Update — Medication Errors Happen to Pets Too
        • FDA — Properly Store Medications to Keep Your Pet Safe
        • FDA — Don’t Expose Pets to Prescription Topical Fluorouracil
        • AVMA policy — Use of Prescription Drugs in Veterinary Medicine

modules.title: Final Assessment
modules.content:
Twelve questions across all eight medication-safety domains. One question at a time, immediate feedback with an explanation, and an explicit pass mark of 80 percent — 10 of 12 correct. You can retake it as many times as you need.

Medication scope — every module

You do

  • Recognize the medication, its risk class, and what the order is asking for.
  • Verify the DVM order, the Pet’s identity, the label, the concentration, and the ordered math.
  • Prepare and label exactly as ordered, with hand hygiene, clean technique, and the right controls.
  • Administer only when authorized for your role, then monitor, document, teach back, and escalate.

You do not

  • Diagnose, prescribe, or select a medication.
  • Choose or change a dose, route, frequency, formulation, or duration.
  • Substitute a product, recalculate around a mismatch, or “fix” an order yourself.
  • Proceed past anything unclear, missing, mismatched, expired, damaged, or outside your role.

If anything does not match, stop and escalate to the DVM or RVT — do not correct the order yourself. Veterinary prescription drugs are restricted by federal law to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian and are to be used or prescribed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship (AVMA prescription-drug policy). Veterinary technicians and assistants work under the supervision of a licensed veterinarian and cannot diagnose, prescribe, or perform acts prohibited by the state practice act (AVMA — veterinary technicians and assistants).

Before you begin

How this assessment works

Questions appear one at a time with a progress indicator. Feedback and the explanation appear the moment you answer, and you can move back through questions you have already answered. Nothing is timed.

The pass mark for this assessment is 80 percent. This threshold applies to this assessment only — it is not a universal Hannah threshold, and it does not replace your hospital's competency policy or your state practice act.

When you finish, a remediation panel lists the safety domains you missed and the module to revisit. Missing a critical safety domain — order verification, concentration and dose verification, patient identity, look-alike and sound-alike names, hazardous drugs, controlled substances, adverse-reaction escalation, near-miss response or abbreviation and decimal risk — requires remediation before you perform the task unsupervised, regardless of the overall percentage.

Scope reminder for every item

Every correct answer on this assessment sits inside the assistant and technician role: recognize, verify, prepare, administer only when authorized, monitor, document, communicate, escalate. No item asks you to choose a medication, a dose, a route or a frequency, and none of these items is a prescribing decision.

quiz.q: Part 1 · Order verificationA medication order for a canine patient lists the Pet, the drug and the amount, but no route. What do you do?
opts: Hold the medication and clarify the route with the DVM or RVT before anything is prepared.
Give it by mouth, because oral is the most common route.
Use the route from the same medication on the previous visit.
Prepare it now and ask about the route at administration.
quiz.exp: Route is part of the directions for use. FDA's extra-label guidance lists species and animal identification, dosage, frequency, route and duration among required directions, so an order without a route is incomplete. Hold and clarify; do not infer it.

quiz.q: Part 1 · Order verificationAn order reads “5.0 mg.” What is the safest response?
opts: Ask for the order to be clarified or rewritten per policy, because a trailing zero can be misread as a tenfold higher dose.
Prepare 5 mg, since the trailing zero does not change the value.
Prepare 50 mg, because the zero indicates tens.
Round to the nearest whole number and continue.
quiz.exp: FDA warns that “5.0 mg” can be misread as “50 mg” and that a missing leading zero turns “.5 mg” into “5 mg.” Both are tenfold risks. The value may well be 5 mg, but you clarify rather than assume.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Concentration and doseThe order specifies an oral suspension at 50 mg/mL. The bottle in your hand reads 25 mg/mL. What do you do?
opts: Stop and escalate the concentration mismatch to the DVM or RVT without preparing anything.
Double the volume so the total milligrams match the order.
Halve the volume to stay on the safe side.
Prepare the ordered volume from the bottle you have and note the difference in the record.
quiz.exp: Recalculating around a mismatch is a substitution you are not authorized to make. You verify DVM-authorized math; changing a product or a volume is prescribing. Stop, escalate, and let the DVM issue a corrected order.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Patient identityWhich is the strongest patient-identity check before a medication?
opts: Compare Pet name, species, signalment, the weight the order was written on, the encounter, the Member or Pet Parent, and the cage or board identifier against the order and the label — before preparation and again at the Pet.
Confirm the Pet's name with whoever is closest to the cage.
Match the cage card to the treatment board once at the start of the shift.
Check the Pet's name and the drug name on the label.
quiz.exp: Wrong drug, wrong dose and wrong frequency are all reportable medication-error scenarios, and every one of them can start with a patient-identity gap. Identity is checked twice: at preparation and again at the Pet.

quiz.q: Part 3 · CommunicationA verbal order sounds like one drug, but the chart context suggests a different, similarly named medication. What happens next?
opts: Read the order back, say the drug name and strength out loud, and get explicit confirmation before proceeding.
Prepare the one that fits the chart context, since that is clinically sensible.
Prepare the one you heard, because the DVM said it.
Ask a colleague which one they would prepare.
quiz.exp: FDA describes a verbal-order mix-up between two similarly named products that harmed a dog. Read-back with the name and strength spoken aloud is the control for look-alike and sound-alike names, and ISMP maintains a confused-drug-name list for exactly this risk.

quiz.q: Part 3 · Aseptic practiceWhen should hand hygiene happen in a medication task?
opts: Immediately before the aseptic preparation task and immediately before touching the patient.
Only after handling the patient, to protect yourself.
Once at the start of the medication round.
Only when hands are visibly soiled.
quiz.exp: CDC recommends cleaning hands immediately before touching a patient and before performing an aseptic task. Medication preparation is an aseptic task, so hand hygiene happens before it and again before patient contact.

quiz.q: Part 3 · Injection and sharps safetyWhat does “One Needle, One Syringe, Only One Time” mean?
opts: A needle and syringe are used for one patient and one entry into a medication, then discarded — never reused across patients or re-entered into a vial.
One needle per shift is acceptable if it is capped between uses.
You may reuse a syringe on the same patient with a new needle for any purpose.
It applies only to controlled substances.
quiz.exp: CDC uses this rule to summarize safe injection practice. Alongside it, OSHA advises not passing used sharps between workers, not recapping, shearing or breaking contaminated needles, and disposing of them immediately in a puncture-resistant sharps container.

quiz.q: Part 4 · Hazardous drugsA hazardous oral medication arrives for a patient and the required PPE is not available in the designated area. What do you do?
opts: Do not handle it outside the protocol — escalate so the hazardous-drug workflow, PPE and spill supplies are in place first.
Handle it quickly with gloves you already have on, since it is only a tablet.
Move it to a quiet area and prepare it there to limit exposure to others.
Split the task with a colleague so each person's exposure is halved.
quiz.exp: NIOSH states that veterinary healthcare employees handling hazardous drugs may face health risks and recommends a protective program; OSHA's hazardous-drug guidance applies to veterinary practices; and USP <800> applies wherever patients, workers or the environment may be exposed. Missing PPE is a stop-and-escalate condition.

quiz.q: Part 4 · Controlled substancesA controlled-substance log entry is missing the witness initials for a wasted amount. What is the safest action?
opts: Notify the authorized DVM, RVT or manager per policy and correct it through the approved documentation process.
Add your own initials as the witness so the log balances.
Ask a colleague to initial it now as if they had witnessed it.
Leave it and mention it at the next inventory count.
quiz.exp: AAHA's controlled-substance materials support DEA recordkeeping and include inventory reconciliation and near-miss incident logs. Backfilling or borrowing a witness signature falsifies a federal record. Escalate the discrepancy instead.

quiz.q: Part 5 · Monitoring and escalationA Pet vomits and develops facial swelling shortly after an authorized medication. What do you do first?
opts: Stay with the Pet if it is safe, escalate to the DVM or RVT immediately, and record the times and what you observed.
Look up the medication's side-effect profile so your report is complete.
Give an antihistamine you have seen used for reactions before.
Wait ten minutes to see whether the signs worsen.
quiz.exp: FDA lists side effects such as vomiting, diarrhea, colic and seizures among reportable adverse events. You do not need a diagnosis to escalate: recognize, escalate immediately, preserve the evidence, and document facts and times.

quiz.q: Part 5 · Member communicationA Member asks whether they can give their own pain reliever to their Pet. What do you say?
opts: Explain that human medication should not be given to a Pet unless the veterinarian directs it, and offer to get an answer from the hospital.
Suggest a small dose is usually fine for a Pet that size.
Say that most human medications are safe if given with food.
Tell them you are not allowed to answer and end the conversation.
quiz.exp: FDA advises Members and Pet Parents not to give human medications to an animal unless directed by the veterinarian, and to store human and animal medications separately. Routing the question to the DVM keeps you inside your scope without leaving the Member without a path.

quiz.q: Part 5 · Near-miss responseYou catch a wrong concentration before anything reaches the Pet. The corrected order is given safely. What should happen to the catch?
opts: Report it internally as a near-miss with the facts, the times and the condition that made it possible, so the system can be fixed.
Nothing — no patient was harmed, so there is nothing to report.
Mention it verbally at the end of the week if it comes up.
Record it only if the same thing happens again.
quiz.exp: FDA encourages reporting all medication errors, including those not associated with an adverse event, so the agency can monitor and help prevent future errors. A near-miss is a free lesson: report the condition, not the person.
